spec.title: Inside the Power Cell
spec.subtitle: Exploring how batteries store, move, and release energy
spec.notes: Every gadget I own runs on them, yet for years I never asked: how does a battery actually work? This deck is my attempt to trace that question from the outside in - starting with what happens at the atomic level when energy gets stored and released. We'll look at the actual chemistry, the circuit that makes it possible, and the tradeoffs between different battery types. The goal is not just to explain, but to build an intuitive picture I can carry forward.

slides.brief: Introduction to how rechargeable batteries store, move, and release energy, set in a sketch notebook style.

spec.title: The Charging Circuit
spec.notes: When we plug in to charge, the external power supply becomes the pump that pushes electrons against their natural tendency. Electrons accumulate at the anode—the negative terminal—while positive ions move through the electrolyte. This charge separation is the battery's stored energy.
spec.caption: During charging, external power forces electrons to the anode and drives cations through the electrolyte, reversing natural flow.

slides.brief: A drawn circuit diagram showing how external power pushes electrons and forces ions to move from cathode to anode.

spec.title: Energy Density Comparison
spec.takeaway: Lithium-ion delivers 5× more energy per kilogram than traditional lead-acid batteries.
spec.notes: Energy density—the amount of energy a battery can store relative to its weight—is the key reason lithium-ion dominates portable electronics. Lead-acid, the oldest rechargeable chemistry, weighs five times as much for the same capacity as lithium-ion. This gap explains why your smartphone battery weighs just a few ounces rather than pounds. NiMH sits in the middle, which is why it replaced NiCd in early portable devices but lost ground to lithium-ion as our devices grew thinner and more demanding.

slides.brief: A column chart comparing energy density across lead-acid, NiMH, and lithium-ion battery types.

spec.title: Inside a Lithium-Ion Cell
spec.notes: Show a real cross-section photo from a reputable open-source source. Explain each component in plain language, linking back to the charging diagram on slide 2.

image.query: lithium ion battery cell internal structure

bullets.text: Anode (graphite) stores lithium ions during discharge
Electrolyte conducts lithium ions while insulating electrons
Separator prevents short-circuit while allowing ion flow

slides.brief: A photo and key bullet points detailing the anode, cathode, electrolyte, and separator.

spec.title: Charge-Discharge Cycle
spec.notes: This slide visualizes the reversible reactions that let a battery be used many times. Emphasize the simplicity: charge pushes ions one way, discharge lets them return.

steps.heading: Apply Power
steps.text: External voltage forces electrons toward the anode.

steps.heading: Ion Migration
steps.text: Lithium ions travel through the electrolyte to the anode.

steps.heading: Store Energy
steps.text: Chemical bonds at the anode hold the ions (charged state).

steps.heading: Use Device
steps.text: When a load is connected, ions flow back, releasing electrons.

steps.heading: Repeat
steps.text: Re-charging reverses the flow, restoring the original state.

slides.brief: A step-by-step process flow explaining reversible chemical reactions during use and recharge.

spec.title: Common Rechargeable Chemistries
spec.notes: Give a quick comparison that high-school students can remember: Li-Ion = light & powerful, NiMH = middle ground, Lead-Acid = heavy & cheap.

cards.heading: Lithium-Ion
cards.text: Highest energy density, low self-discharge, used in phones, laptops, and EVs.

cards.heading: Nickel-Metal Hydride
cards.text: Moderate density, no memory effect, found in hybrid cars and older digital cameras.

cards.heading: Lead-Acid
cards.text: Heavy, inexpensive, high surge current, common in car starters and backup power.

slides.brief: Cards outlining lithium-ion, nickel-metal hydride, and lead-acid batteries with their typical applications.

spec.title: Powering Tomorrow
spec.subtitle: From Classroom Curiosity to Sustainable Innovation
spec.notes: Wrap up with three takeaways: 1) Batteries store energy by moving ions, 2) Chemistry decides performance trade‑offs, 3) Emerging chemistries (solid‑state, flow) will shape the future. Invite students to keep asking how everyday tech works.
